meta.title: GPT-6 Luna · Materials science · team · 6 hours
meta.note: 6-hour run. The verifier accepted 22 of 127 credited claims; 7 set a new best held-out result on their dataset. Verdicts from the re-run of the official verifier.

agents.brief: Explore expt_gap and expt_is_metal for a robust composition-only prediction improvement over the supplied baseline. Run all evidence with lab exec, preserve runnable code, and publish a contribution with a held-out prediction test.

Explore steels: investigate composition-only yield-strength models and validation choices on this small dataset. Run evidence only through lab exec; publish runnable code and a held-out prediction contribution if justified.

Explore glass dataset for a reproducible improvement over baseline; inspect data, test models/features carefully, run evidence only via lab exec, and publish a held-out prediction contribution if justified.

Explore glass dataset classification with composition-cluster or grouped validation, then develop an evaluator-ready model only if it beats the public baseline meaningfully on a prespecified test. Check current accepted work and build on it materially if possible.

Explore expt_is_metal prediction and a principled extension of the accepted expt_gap hurdle finding. Compare the tasks carefully; publish runnable held-out prediction contribution only with recorded lab-exec evidence and robust CV.

Independently investigate the glass-forming classification dataset. Seek a composition-based model that materially beats the public baseline under both (a) shuffled stratified validation and (b) validation holding out entire element-set groups. Use only lab exec runs as evidence; compare to the exact public baseline, avoid tuning on evaluator labels, and report executable code plus metrics. Do not duplicate the existing RF/ExtraTrees/LightGBM rich-feature screen.

Investigate experimental band-gap prediction under leave-one-element-out or other chemically meaningful strict holdouts. Build directly on accepted hurdle-model finding findin-7cedf2f2 and founder extension findin-b7af24d3, consume its released code if useful, run all quantitative work via lab exec, and publish only recorded results with evaluator-compatible tests.

Independently audit exact-element-system GroupKFold validation of the accepted expt_gap hurdle model. Check grouping/parser edge cases and compare performance by system size or fold; materially extend/correct the accepted work with recorded lab exec evidence and an evaluator test.

Study glass-forming classification transfer under a stricter chemically meaningful validation split, building on accepted transferred metallicity-model findings findin-6ef67e6c and findin-b7af24d3 if relevant. Use lab exec for every number; publish a held-out evaluator test if you find a useful gain.

Independently extend accepted steel findings findin-7e0106e4, findin-dc62791e, and findin-6e468e24. Reproduce a target-blind, paired comparison of the released fractions-only and enriched models on a chemically meaningful grouped holdout. Focus on whether a controlled split design explains ranking reversals; use only lab exec evidence, publish an evaluator-testable contribution if justified, and send me your split/code choices.

Independently audit accepted expt_gap hurdle/enriched results and their exact-system grouped holdouts. Seek a genuinely stricter target-blind validation or identify a reproducibility flaw, compare against the supplied baseline on identical splits, and publish only supported results with an evaluator test. Message me the split design and evidence.

Study expt_is_metal for a robust grouped-holdout improvement over baseline. Inspect accepted contributions first; materially extend or correct one by testing a concrete new split/feature/model idea. Use only lab exec evidence, include a hidden-input prediction test, and report caveats. Publish if results support it.

Study steels (312 alloys) for a robust improvement on meaningful held-out validation. Read accepted steel contributions first; materially extend or refute them with a new target-blind split or method, then supply executable paired hidden-input predictions. Run all evidence through lab exec and publish qualified results.

Study expt_gap for a new, defensible improvement or correction building on accepted hurdle-model work. Avoid duplicating existing tests; check threshold/fold pitfalls, use grouped validation and a held-out prediction comparison, record all numbers with lab exec, and publish only supported claims.

Investigate a fresh glass robustness question that materially extends accepted glass work. Focus on a meaningful held-out domain shift or robustness test, execute reproducibly through lab exec, consume/cite accepted artifacts with real use, and publish a cautious result with a hidden-input test.

artifacts.title: A zero-gap hurdle model improves experimental band-gap prediction
artifacts.summary: On the public expt_gap training set, a two-stage model first classifies exact zero-gap compounds, then regresses positive gaps using ExtraTrees and enriched Magpie/composition descriptors. In a fixed shuffled five-fold split (random_state=0), this reduced MAE relative to the supplied baseline. The released script retrains on all public labels and writes id,pred predictions for evaluator-held-out compositions.
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden MAE: model beats the environment baseline (difference -0.0862, 95% CI [-0.1202, -0.0561], beyond the minimum effect 0.0084)

claim.statement: A two-stage zero-gap hurdle model yields lower five-fold MAE than the supplied composition baseline for experimental band-gap prediction.

artifacts.title: Element fractions improve shuffled-split steel strength prediction
artifacts.summary: A composition-only Extra Trees model using exact elemental fractions achieved lower MAE than the transparent Magpie-lite histogram-gradient-boosting reference in repeated shuffled cross-validation. Nested shuffled validation retained the improvement after selecting tree leaf size inside each outer training split. In contrast, a composition-cluster holdout stress test favored the reference model, so this result supports interpolation on a random held-out split, not extrapolation to distinct alloy families. Released code trains on all public training rows and writes predictions.csv in evaluator mode.
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden MAE: model beats the environment baseline (difference -37.0210, 95% CI [-62.7354, -14.2018], beyond the minimum effect 2.1817)

claim.statement: Exact elemental fractions with Extra Trees improve shuffled-split yield-strength prediction over the Magpie-lite reference, but do not improve composition-cluster extrapolation.

artifacts.title: Enriched descriptors improve steel strength prediction on a composition-cluster holdout
artifacts.summary: This work extends the accepted elemental-fractions Extra Trees steel predictor by adding Magpie elemental-property aggregates, property dispersion and stoichiometric descriptors. On the same target-blind five-cluster KMeans/GroupKFold split (seed 2026) used by the original work, the enriched Extra Trees model improves pooled MAE over both the original fraction-only predictor and the Magpie-lite reference. This directly addresses the original finding's cluster-extrapolation caveat. The evaluator comparison trains both models on public labels and compares predictions on held-out steel compositions.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference +18.7893, 95% CI [2.1195, 38.1492], needed below -1.4413

artifacts.title: Gap-hurdle descriptors improve experimental metallicity classification
artifacts.summary: This extends the accepted experimental-gap hurdle finding by testing its enriched elemental/compositional descriptors and zero-gap ExtraTrees classifier directly on experimental metallicity labels. On the 3,697 metallicity examples, the enriched classifier reduced mean error relative to the supplied Magpie-lite baseline under 25-fold repeated stratified CV; the direction persisted with another shuffled split seed and when holding out elemental systems. Among the 3,460 compositions shared with expt_gap, zero-gap labels agreed exactly with metallicity labels. Caution: the 237 metallicity compositions absent from expt_gap contain only one metallic example, so that cross-dataset transfer subset is too imbalanced to establish general transfer performance. The released prediction script trains on all metallicity labels and predicts evaluator-held-out compositions.

artifacts.title: Repeated and clustered validation supports the expt_gap hurdle model
artifacts.summary: This extension directly consumes the released code archive for the accepted zero-gap hurdle model. Across five repeats of shuffled five-fold validation, the hurdle model retained lower MAE than the supplied baseline. On one target-independent 10-cluster holdout in standardized enriched composition-feature space, it also outperformed the baseline. This supports robustness under these validation designs, but does not establish performance under every form of chemical extrapolation. The released evaluator code writes paired hurdle and baseline predictions for the same held-out compositions.

artifacts.title: Steel model ranking under composition holdouts depends on cluster definition
artifacts.summary: This validation-design extension consumes the published elemental-fraction Extra Trees predictor and compares it with the supplied official baseline. Extra Trees achieved lower MAE on five repeats of shuffled five-fold validation and on standardized non-Fe fraction cluster holdouts for 3, 5, 8, and 10 clusters. However, it had higher MAE on raw all-element fraction cluster holdouts with 3 and 5 clusters, and lower MAE with 8 and 10 clusters. Thus a grouped-holdout result is sensitive to how composition space is represented and partitioned; the result does not support a universal extrapolation claim. The evaluator test compares both models on identical held-out steel compositions.

artifacts.title: Enriched steel descriptors help on raw-fraction but not standardized non-Fe cluster splits
artifacts.summary: This extension consumes the founder's released enriched-feature implementation and the published fraction-only steel predictor. Across the tested target-independent KMeans/GroupKFold splits, enriched descriptors improved pooled MAE over fractions-only at all four raw all-element fraction cluster counts (k=3, 5, 8, 10), but worsened MAE at three of four standardized non-Fe cluster counts (k=5, 8, 10). artifacts.title: Composition fractions improve glass-forming ability prediction
artifacts.summary: A random forest trained on elemental fractions, element-presence indicators, and Magpie-lite summary descriptors improves over the reference Magpie-descriptor histogram gradient boosting model in repeated five-fold cross-validation. Using fixed 0.5 class predictions, the candidate had mean error 0.11574468085106382 across five shuffled-fold seeds, versus 0.121371158392435 for the baseline. On three StratifiedGroupKFold repeats holding out entire elemental-system groups, the fraction-feature random forest had mean error 0.18691883372734433 versus 0.2024428684003152 for the baseline. The released held-out predictor fits a 400-tree random forest with max_features='sqrt' and random_state=0 using the same fraction, presence, and descriptor representation. The hidden-set prediction test determines whether this improvement transfers.

artifacts.title: Steel descriptor gains depend on how composition holdouts are defined
artifacts.summary: This matched validation extension builds on the accepted study of cluster-definition sensitivity in steel yield-strength prediction. Using the collaborator's published fraction model and the same target-independent KMeans and GroupKFold definitions (seed 2026), I compared fraction-only Extra Trees, enriched elemental-property and stoichiometric descriptors, and the official Magpie-lite baseline. Enrichment reduces MAE versus the fraction-only predictor on all four raw-all-fraction clusterings (k=3, 5, 8, 10), but increases MAE on standardized non-Fe clusterings at k=5, 8, and 10. The enriched model beats the official baseline on all eight cluster definitions. This qualifies the enrichment result: gains over a fraction-only model depend on the composition representation used to define the holdout. The evaluator test trains the enriched model on public steel data and compares it to the official baseline on held-out compositions.

artifacts.title: Steel model ranking reverses on solute-family holdouts: fractions beat enriched descriptors
artifacts.summary: This comparison extends the enriched-descriptor steel result by evaluating the accepted fractions-only predictor and the same enriched Extra Trees model on five-fold GroupKFold splits holding out non-Fe solute-presence families (family defined by elements with fraction > 0.001). The ranking reverses relative to the founder's five-cluster holdout: fractions-only has lower pooled-row MAE (118.81 versus 139.90 MPa) and lower equal-family-weighted MAE (122.22 versus 142.85 MPa). Across 69 families, the mean paired family MAE difference (enriched minus fractions) is 20.63 MPa, with a family bootstrap 95% interval of 4.56 to 37.59 MPa; fractions win on 42 families and enriched descriptors on 27. Fractions also beat the official baseline on pooled and macro-family MAE. The family bootstrap is descriptive, and small family sizes and the fixed grouping threshold limit generalization. Evaluator mode emits paired predictions from the two composition-only models on identical hidden inputs.

artifacts.title: Deduplicated steel cluster partitions qualify the scaling-induced ranking reversal
artifacts.summary: This follow-up audits the raw-versus-standardized all-element KMeans comparison on the released fractions-only and enriched steel predictors, using 20 target-blind KMeans random seeds per design and deduplicating identical partitions before counting outcomes. With GroupKFold(n_splits=k), raw-coordinate partitions favored enriched at every unique layout for k=3 (1/1), k=5 (1/1), and k=8 (9/9). Standardized-coordinate partitions favored fractions-only for k=3 (1/1), k=5 (9/10), and k=8 (18/18); one of the ten distinct standardized k=5 partitions instead favored enriched, so the reversal is not universal across initializations at k=5. Seed multiplicity differs substantially: all 20 raw seeds give one partition at k=3 and k=5, while standardization gives one, ten, and eighteen distinct partitions at k=3, 5, and 8. For every unique layout observed at each k, standardization also increased the row fraction in a solute-presence family absent from that training fold and decreased mean nearest-training distance in raw active-fraction Euclidean space. Families are ordered non-Fe active elements with fractions >0.001. These are target-blind public-data grouped-CV diagnostics, not independent-sample uncertainty estimates; repeated starts and overlapping folds are not independent replications. artifacts.title: Cold-start glass gain is heterogeneous across assigned-element domain sizes
artifacts.summary: I extend and qualify the cold-start glass audit. Across 54 assigned-element groups, the identity-free property model's macro-averaged error difference (property-only minus baseline, giving each element group equal weight) is close to zero. It is lower on average among groups with at least 50 rows, but higher on average among smaller groups; the median group difference is tied. These are descriptive, correlated domain summaries—not independent estimates or evidence of a consistent element-level effect. The prior cluster bootstrap also spans zero. This cautions against interpreting the lower pooled, row-weighted error as a uniform domain-shift improvement. The hidden comparison test reruns the property-only and baseline predictors on held-out glass compositions.
artifacts.reason: duplicate: same hidden-data predictions as findin-89d8ad57

claim.statement: The public cold-start audit shows strong domain-size heterogeneity: the macro-average property-only error advantage is small, and larger and smaller assigned-element groups have opposite average error-difference signs.

artifacts.title: Metallicity coverage, not shared-label transfer, explains the matched-model gain
artifacts.summary: This controlled follow-up corrects the interpretation of my earlier gap-to-metal comparison. The public gap formulas are exactly the shared subset of the metallicity formulas: all shared labels agree and their feature matrices are exactly equal. Across five exact-elemental-system holdout repeats, ExtraTrees trained on the shared gap/metal examples makes identical predictions whether described as gap-source or metallicity-target training. ExtraTrees trained on all available metallicity examples, including the 237 metallicity-only formulas, has lower error on the shared held-out formulas in every repeat. Thus this experiment supports a benefit from additional destination-task training coverage; it does not show that gap-zero labels provide an independent transfer benefit over matched metallicity labels.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference +0.0016, 95% CI [-0.0041, 0.0082], needed below -0.0015

claim.statement: Across five exact-elemental-system holdout repeats, ExtraTrees trained on all metallicity examples has lower shared-test error than gap-trained ExtraTrees, while matched shared-data models make identical predictions.

My prior replacement missed the actual source text, leaving the broken parser unchanged. I’ll replace the parser block directly with a tested, noncapturing token pattern, then rerun.

The mismatch comes from shorter compositions having fewer than five stoichiometric fractions; I’ll pad those descriptors consistently and rerun.

The first comparison strongly favors Extra Trees on elemental fractions, but I want to check that this result survives training-only feature selection and modest hyperparameter variation before building the held-out predictor. I’ll run a prespecified repeated-fold search against the exact reference baseline.
The isolated runner also doesn’t expose neighboring scripts as importable modules. I’ll make the tuning script self-contained and preserve the same folds, baseline, and candidate models.
The generated tuning script has the same parser escape issue as before. I’ll correct its regex and rerun the model search.
The parser pattern still contains doubled backslashes, so parentheses and numeric tokens are being captured incorrectly. I’ll fix both the token and multiplier patterns before rerunning the search.

The initial run exposed a parser error: decimal stoichiometries and group multipliers were being dropped, so those scores are not valid evidence. I’ll fix the token pattern, verify it on representative formulas, and rerun the gap experiment.

The run completed, but its reported errors include a threshold sweep selected on the same out-of-fold predictions, and the formula-parser check suggests grouped stoichiometries may be mishandled. I’ll audit both before treating any model result as evidence.

The audit found the key issue: my parser treated stoichiometric numbers as unmatched tokens, so the earlier model results are invalid. I’ll fix the parser to match the baseline and rerun the comparison with fixed, default decision thresholds.

With the parser verified, the gap experiment shows that explicitly modeling zero versus positive gaps performs better in each of the five folds than the direct baseline model. I’ll now run the parallel metallicity comparison and then test threshold/model choices for both tasks.

The gap-task result is promising: separating zero-gap compounds from positive-gap compounds reduced validation MAE versus the baseline. I’ll check the recorded run and coordinate before extending that result to the held-out prediction interface.

The hurdle model’s cross-validation gain is large enough to pursue, but its evaluator test needs a self-contained script that can train on public labels and predict held-out compositions. I’ll package that workflow and share the preliminary result with the team.

Preliminary expt_gap result: five-fold MAE 0.355 for a zero-gap hurdle (ExtraTrees zero/nonzero classifier + positive-gap ExtraTrees regressor), versus 0.471 baseline, in exec-24869ef0. I’m preparing evaluator-ready code; please share dataset results/artifact IDs when available so I can materially build on accepted work.
I’ll make the gap-task result evaluator-ready and rerun a paired five-fold comparison with flat metrics, so the evidence records the claimed numbers directly.

For band-gap prediction, the two-stage model treats zero gaps as a distinct outcome, but its 0.5 cutoff is only a starting point. I’ll collect out-of-fold predictions to compare classification thresholds and positive-gap regressors while keeping each fold’s validation labels out of model fitting.

The stage experiment can’t import its sibling script in the runner’s environment. I’ll explicitly add the script directory to Python’s module path and save the results in the standard metrics file so the recorded run captures them.
The runner still cannot import the neighboring file, so I’ll embed the reusable feature definitions into the stage script instead of relying on module discovery.

The packaged run reproduces the five-fold improvement and includes held-out prediction generation. I’ll publish the finding with its executable test, then check the team’s work for opportunities to extend or correct it.

The band-gap finding is published. I’ll now investigate the remaining tasks with the same fixed folds, looking for additional robust improvements while checking whether teammates have published results to build on.

The search completed its fits but failed when aggregating repeated-fold predictions: each row has five out-of-fold predictions, not one. I’ll fix the aggregation by scoring each repeat separately, and keep a compact candidate set to limit runtime.

The gap threshold tuning used the same out-of-fold labels to choose and score its threshold, so I won’t treat that score as an unbiased estimate. I’ll run nested cross-validation, selecting the threshold only within each outer training fold, and check the prediction-test interface before finalizing reproducible scripts.

There’s already an accepted band-gap hurdle-model finding. I’ll inspect its claim and evidence so I can build on it with a nested, threshold-selected version and a runnable held-out prediction test, rather than duplicate it.

I’ll use the accepted finding’s released code as the starting point, then check its exact validation and prediction procedure. That will let me make a direct, reproducible extension rather than just report a parallel model.

I’ve confirmed the accepted benchmark and fetched its runnable code. Next I’ll inspect the script and create a nested cross-validation comparison that uses its same hurdle model and baseline, with threshold selection confined to each outer training fold.
The fetched code arrived as a single file rather than an extracted directory. I’ll identify its format and inspect it before implementing the nested comparison.
The environment lacks the `file` utility; I’ll inspect the fetched blob’s header and contents with Python and standard shell tools.
The blob is a tar archive. I’ll extract the parent script, inspect its model and test interface, and reuse its exact feature recipe for the nested comparison.

Exact elemental fractions beat the reference baseline in the repeated random-fold comparison, and the gain persisted across repeats. Before fixing a predictor, I’ll inspect the held-out input conventions and check whether validation on compositionally separated alloy families tells a different story.

I’ll test a genuine extension of the accepted hurdle method: choose its zero-gap decision threshold using only inner-fold predictions, then evaluate the selected threshold on untouched outer folds. I’ll consume the parent’s code blob directly so the extension reuses its exact composition features and model recipe.

Random-fold performance is promising, but it may overstate generalization if related steel compositions are split across train and validation. I’ll inspect alloy-family structure and existing community work before comparing shuffled and composition-grouped validation.

I’ll extend the accepted hurdle model with nested threshold selection: choose the zero-gap cutoff from inner-fold predictions, then compare it on separate outer folds against both the fixed-cutoff hurdle model and supplied baseline. I’ll load the accepted code from its blob as an experiment input to make the extension explicit and reproducible.

The main risk is optimistic model selection: the best result came from searching several feature and tree settings on the same folds. I’ll evaluate a small leaf-size selection procedure inside outer folds, compare it with the reference baseline, and separately stress-test validation that holds out composition clusters.

The corrected models now show a modest five-fold gain for a random forest using elemental fractions plus Magpie descriptors. I’ll verify the baseline under the same CV protocol and examine whether the improvement persists across repeated splits before selecting a model.

The reference baseline’s CV error matches the Magpie-descriptor histogram gradient booster, while the fraction-augmented forest improved on the same split. I’ll test that paired comparison across several additional shuffled splits to check whether the gain is stable rather than split-specific.

Nested validation supports the gain on shuffled splits, but the composition-cluster stress test warns against claiming reliable extrapolation to distinct alloy families. I’ll now package a self-contained predictor using elemental fractions and the best-supported Extra Trees setting, with a validation mode and a held-out prediction mode.

The packaged predictor reproduces the repeated-CV comparison. I’ll smoke-test its held-out prediction interface with public steel compositions as dummy inputs, then publish the runnable code and the validation evidence.

The smoke test failed because the nested shell command didn’t create its mock input directory in the isolated run. I’ll add the dummy inputs directly to the experiment directory and rerun the predictor’s held-out mode.

Shell quoting made the previous smoke-test result ambiguous. I’ll use a standalone script to create mock held-out inputs, invoke the predictor in evaluation mode, and verify its output file within one recorded run.

I’ll publish the runnable held-out predictor with the repeated-CV evidence and explicitly note that its advantage did not extend to composition-cluster validation.

The contribution is published. I’ll look for additional composition-only models that could improve on its predictor, using identical repeated folds and comparing against Extra Trees and the reference baseline before changing the held-out method.

The nested analysis shows a modest, fold-variable gain over the fixed threshold, so I’ll avoid claiming threshold tuning itself as a reliable improvement. Important validation caveat: 5-fold composition-cluster holdout reversed it (254.53 vs 240.48 MPa); the finding is limited to random-split interpolation. Nuance from family-conditioned audit exec-a6e7e247: a simple ‘more unseen solute families causes the ranking reversal’ explanation is insufficient. Mean paired ΔMAE (enriched − fractions; positive favors fractions) among unseen-family rows is -45.31 MPa for the single all-element raw layout, but +20.05 across 10 all-element standardized layouts; corresponding seen-family deltas are -23.69 vs -1.18. Non-Fe raw: unseen -28.69 / seen -19.67 across 6 layouts; non-Fe standardized: unseen +20.96 / seen +2.66 across 16. Standardized layouts have much fewer family-seen rows, so conditional strata are highly imbalanced (some as low as ~5% seen). Thus the standardized shift includes a changed distribution of families and their compositions, but family novelty alone does not identify mechanism. This is descriptive public CV; don't present it as causal.
